claim: Ena/VASP proteins were previously thought to antagonize efficient cell motility.
source: Cell migration entails networks and bundles of actin filaments termed lamellipodia and microspikes or filopodia, respectively, as well as focal adhesions, all of which recruit Ena/VASP family members hitherto thought to antagonize efficient cell motility.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information, referencing prior understanding in the field.

claim: Ena/VASP proteins act as positive regulators of migration in different murine cell lines.
source: However, we find these proteins to act as positive regulators of migration in different murine cell lines.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss of Ena/VASP proteins reduced lamellipodial actin assembly.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss of Ena/VASP proteins reduced lamellipodial actin assembly and perturbed lamellipodial architecture, as evidenced by changed network geometry as well as reduction of filament length and number that was accompanied by abnormal Arp2/3 complex and heterodimeric capping protein accumulation.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data including electron tomography and immunofluorescence.

claim: Loss of Ena/VASP proteins perturbed lamellipodial architecture with changed network geometry.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss of Ena/VASP proteins reduced lamellipodial actin assembly and perturbed lamellipodial architecture, as evidenced by changed network geometry as well as reduction of filament length and number that was accompanied by abnormal Arp2/3 complex and heterodimeric capping protein accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data showing altered filament angles and organization.

claim: Loss of Ena/VASP proteins resulted in reduction of filament length and number in lamellipodia.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss of Ena/VASP proteins reduced lamellipodial actin assembly and perturbed lamellipodial architecture, as evidenced by changed network geometry as well as reduction of filament length and number that was accompanied by abnormal Arp2/3 complex and heterodimeric capping protein accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography measurements showing shorter filaments in EVM-KO cells.

claim: Loss of Ena/VASP proteins was accompanied by abnormal Arp2/3 complex accumulation.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss of Ena/VASP proteins reduced lamellipodial actin assembly and perturbed lamellipodial architecture, as evidenced by changed network geometry as well as reduction of filament length and number that was accompanied by abnormal Arp2/3 complex and heterodimeric capping protein accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing increased Arp2/3 complex intensity at lamellipodial tips.

claim: Loss of Ena/VASP proteins was accompanied by abnormal heterodimeric capping protein accumulation.
source: CRISPR/Cas9-mediated loss of Ena/VASP proteins reduced lamellipodial actin assembly and perturbed lamellipodial architecture, as evidenced by changed network geometry as well as reduction of filament length and number that was accompanied by abnormal Arp2/3 complex and heterodimeric capping protein accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data showing increased capping protein intensity at lamellipodial tips.

claim: Loss of Ena/VASP function abolished the formation of microspikes normally embedded in lamellipodia.
source: Loss of Ena/VASP function also abolished the formation of microspikes normally embedded in lamellipodia, but not of filopodia capable of emanating without lamellipodia.
evidence: This is supported by phalloidin staining and fascin immunolabeling showing absence of microspikes in EVM-KO cells.

claim: Loss of Ena/VASP function did not abolish filopodia capable of emanating without lamellipodia.
source: Loss of Ena/VASP function also abolished the formation of microspikes normally embedded in lamellipodia, but not of filopodia capable of emanating without lamellipodia.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing filopodia formation in EVM-KO cells after Arp2/3 inhibition or mDia2 expression.

claim: Ena/VASP-deficiency impaired integrin-mediated adhesion.
source: Ena/VASP-deficiency also impaired integrin-mediated adhesion accompanied by reduced traction forces exerted through these structures.
evidence: This is supported by focal adhesion analysis showing reduced vinculin intensity and FA size in mutant cells.

claim: Ena/VASP-deficiency was accompanied by reduced traction forces.
source: Ena/VASP-deficiency also impaired integrin-mediated adhesion accompanied by reduced traction forces exerted through these structures.
evidence: This is supported by traction force microscopy data showing reduced contractile energy in MVE-KO cells.

claim: The lamellipodium is the major protrusive structure of migrating cells on flat and rigid substrata.
source: The major protrusive structure of migrating cells on flat and rigid substrata is the sheet-like lamellipodium (Letort et al., 2015; Rottner et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Extension of dense and branched actin filaments in the lamellipodium drives its growth and pushes the membrane forward.
source: The extension of dense and branched actin filaments in the lamellipodium drives its growth and pushes the membrane forward (Koestler et al., 2008; Mullins et al., 1998; Pollard and Borisy, 2003; Vinzenz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this mechanism.

claim: Branching by Arp2/3 complex is activated by the WAVE regulatory complex downstream of Rac subfamily GTPase signaling.
source: Branching by Actin-related protein (Arp) 2/3 complex is activated by the WAVE regulatory complex (WRC) downstream of Rac subfamily GTPase signaling (Eden et al., 2002; Ismail et al., 2009; Molinie and Gautreau, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Knockdown or knockout of essential Arp2/3 complex subunits abrogated lamellipodium formation.
source: Consistently, knockdown or knockout of essential Arp2/3 complex (Suraneni et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012) or WRC subunits (Innocenti et al., 2004; Schaks et al., 2018; Steffen et al., 2004) or Rac GTPases (Schaks et al., 2018; Steffen et al., 2013) all abrogated lamellipodium formation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Knockdown or knockout of WRC subunits abrogated lamellipodium formation.
source: Consistently, knockdown or knockout of essential Arp2/3 complex (Suraneni et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012) or WRC subunits (Innocenti et al., 2004; Schaks et al., 2018; Steffen et al., 2004) or Rac GTPases (Schaks et al., 2018; Steffen et al., 2013) all abrogated lamellipodium formation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Knockdown or knockout of Rac GTPases abrogated lamellipodium formation.
source: Consistently, knockdown or knockout of essential Arp2/3 complex (Suraneni et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012) or WRC subunits (Innocenti et al., 2004; Schaks et al., 2018; Steffen et al., 2004) or Rac GTPases (Schaks et al., 2018; Steffen et al., 2013) all abrogated lamellipodium formation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The lateral flow of actin filaments and bundles embedded in the lamellipodium, called microspikes, is driven by actin assembly at the membrane.
source: The lateral flow of actin filaments and bundles embedded in the lamellipodium, called microspikes, is driven by actin assembly at the membrane (Oldenbourg et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: When microspikes transform and protrude beyond the lamellipodium edge, they are called filopodia.
source: When microspikes transform and protrude beyond the lamellipodium edge, they are called filopodia (Small, 1988; Svitkina et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Filopodia can kink and bend, as opposed to microspikes.
source: As opposed to microspikes as integral parts of lamellipodial networks, filopodia can kink and bend (Nemethova et al., 2008), arising independently and even in excess in the absence of lamellipodia (Gupton et al., 2005; Koestler et al., 2013; Steffen et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Filopodia can arise independently and even in excess in the absence of lamellipodia.
source: As opposed to microspikes as integral parts of lamellipodial networks, filopodia can kink and bend (Nemethova et al., 2008), arising independently and even in excess in the absence of lamellipodia (Gupton et al., 2005; Koestler et al., 2013; Steffen et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Filopodia can form around the entire cell periphery and at the dorsal surface.
source: Consistently, filopodia can form around the entire cell periphery and at the dorsal surface (Block et al., 2008; Bohil et al., 2006; Pellegrin and Mellor, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Rates of actin polymerization in microspikes and lamellipodia are indistinguishable from each other.
source: Moreover, rates of actin polymerization in microspikes and lamellipodia are indistinguishable from each other (Lai et al., 2008; Oldenbourg et al., 2000), whereas those in filopodia appear to be regulated independently.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Rates of actin polymerization in filopodia appear to be regulated independently from microspikes and lamellipodia.
source: Moreover, rates of actin polymerization in microspikes and lamellipodia are indistinguishable from each other (Lai et al., 2008; Oldenbourg et al., 2000), whereas those in filopodia appear to be regulated independently.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and logical inference.

claim: Formins are dimeric multi domain proteins that remain tightly associated with growing filament barbed ends while accelerating their growth.
source: Formins are dimeric multi domain proteins that remain tightly associated with growing filament barbed ends while accelerating their growth (Kovar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: mDia2 localizes at lamellipodia and filopodia tips.
source: Several formins such as mDia2 (Block et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2007) and the formin-like family members 2 (FMNL2) and 3 (Block et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2010; Kage et al., 2017; Young et al., 2018) localize at lamellipodia and filopodia tips, and have been implicated in driving these protrusions and cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FMNL2 and FMNL3 localize at lamellipodia and filopodia tips.
source: Several formins such as mDia2 (Block et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2007) and the formin-like family members 2 (FMNL2) and 3 (Block et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2010; Kage et al., 2017; Young et al., 2018) localize at lamellipodia and filopodia tips, and have been implicated in driving these protrusions and cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: mDia2, FMNL2, and FMNL3 have been implicated in driving lamellipodia, filopodia, and cell migration.
source: Several formins such as mDia2 (Block et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2007) and the formin-like family members 2 (FMNL2) and 3 (Block et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2010; Kage et al., 2017; Young et al., 2018) localize at lamellipodia and filopodia tips, and have been implicated in driving these protrusions and cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ena/VASP family proteins localize to sites of active actin assembly including focal adhesions.
source: Ena/VASP family proteins localize to sites of active actin assembly including focal adhesions (FA) (Gertler et al., 1996; Reinhard et al., 1995), stress fibers (Gateva et al., 2014; Rottner et al., 2001; Tojkander et al., 2015), and lamellipodial or filopodial tips (Rottner et al., 1999; Svitkina et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ena/VASP family proteins localize to stress fibers.
source: Ena/VASP family proteins localize to sites of active actin assembly including focal adhesions (FA) (Gertler et al., 1996; Reinhard et al., 1995), stress fibers (Gateva et al., 2014; Rottner et al., 2001; Tojkander et al., 2015), and lamellipodial or filopodial tips (Rottner et al., 1999; Svitkina et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ena/VASP family proteins localize to lamellipodial or filopodial tips.
source: Ena/VASP family proteins localize to sites of active actin assembly including focal adhesions (FA) (Gertler et al., 1996; Reinhard et al., 1995), stress fibers (Gateva et al., 2014; Rottner et al., 2001; Tojkander et al., 2015), and lamellipodial or filopodial tips (Rottner et al., 1999; Svitkina et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Vertebrates harbor three Ena/VASP family members: VASP, Mena, and Evl.
source: Vertebrates harbor Vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein (VASP), mammalian Protein Enabled Homolog (Mena), and Ena-VASP-like protein (Evl).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Ena/VASP protein family.

claim: All Ena/VASP family members are tetramers.
source: All family members are tetramers encompassing domains allowing for interactions with FPPPP-containing proteins, actin monomers, profilin-actin complexes and actin filaments (Bear and Gertler, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Ena/VASP family members have domains allowing for interactions with FPPPP-containing proteins, actin monomers, profilin-actin complexes and actin filaments.
source: All family members are tetramers encompassing domains allowing for interactions with FPPPP-containing proteins, actin monomers, profilin-actin complexes and actin filaments (Bear and Gertler, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Single Ena/VASP tetramers are poorly processive actin polymerases.
source: Single Ena/VASP tetramers are poorly processive actin polymerases, but processivity and resistance against heterodimeric capping protein that stops barbed end growth, increases markedly upon oligomerization or clustering (Breitsprecher et al., 2011a; Breitsprecher et al., 2008; Brühmann et al., 2017; Hansen and Mullins, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Processivity and resistance against capping protein of Ena/VASP increases markedly upon oligomerization or clustering.
source: Single Ena/VASP tetramers are poorly processive actin polymerases, but processivity and resistance against heterodimeric capping protein that stops barbed end growth, increases markedly upon oligomerization or clustering (Breitsprecher et al., 2011a; Breitsprecher et al., 2008; Brühmann et al., 2017; Hansen and Mullins, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Genetic removal of all three Ena/VASP proteins was previously shown to abrogate filopodia formation in neuronal cells.
source: Consistent with their accumulation at filopodia tips, genetic removal of all three Ena/VASP proteins was previously shown to abrogate filopodia formation in neuronal cells (Kwiatkowski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Elimination of VASP in Dictyostelium cells diminishes random motility and chemotaxis.
source: Elimination of the single family member VASP in Dictyostelium cells diminishes random motility and chemotaxis (Han et al., 2002; Litschko et al., 2017) suggesting a stimulatory role VASP on cells migration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VASP accumulation at lamellipodia tips positively correlates with protrusion rates in B16-F1 mouse melanoma cells.
source: Consistently, VASP accumulation at lamellipodia tips was shown to positively correlate with protrusion rates in B16-F1 mouse melanoma cells (Rottner et al., 1999) and fish keratocytes (Lacayo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VASP accumulation at lamellipodia tips positively correlates with protrusion rates in fish keratocytes.
source: Consistently, VASP accumulation at lamellipodia tips was shown to positively correlate with protrusion rates in B16-F1 mouse melanoma cells (Rottner et al., 1999) and fish keratocytes (Lacayo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Genetic inactivation of VASP and Mena or mitochondrial Ena/VASP sequestration in fibroblasts was reported to increase cell migration.
source: On the other hand, genetic inactivation of VASP and Mena or mitochondrial Ena/VASP sequestration in fibroblasts was reported to increase cell migration (Bear et al., 2002; Bear et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Lamellipodia protruded more persistently after interference with Ena/VASP function.
source: This phenotype was explained by lamellipodia protruding more persistently after interference with Ena/VASP function, and containing shorter and more branched filaments.
evidence: This is a reported explanation from prior literature for the increased migration phenotype.

claim: Excess of Ena/VASP generated lamellipodia with longer, less branched filaments.
source: Excess of Ena/VASP, in contrast, generated lamellipodia with longer, less branched filaments, prone to lifting rearwards during membrane ruffling, therefore driving migration less efficiently (Bear et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Ena sequestration in Drosophila haemocytes resulted in slower migration.
source: However, a similar approach yielded opposite results on the migratory behavior of Drosophila haemocytes with slower migration upon Ena sequestration and faster migration rates upon Ena overexpression (Tucker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Ena overexpression in Drosophila haemocytes resulted in faster migration rates.
source: However, a similar approach yielded opposite results on the migratory behavior of Drosophila haemocytes with slower migration upon Ena sequestration and faster migration rates upon Ena overexpression (Tucker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Breast cancer cells overexpressing Mena showed increased motility.
source: The latter observations again resemble the increased motility described for breast cancer cells overexpressing Mena (Philippar et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Ena/VASP proteins are relevant in the movement of Listeria through the host cell cytosol.
source: Despite described controversies concerning motility, the proposed positive regulatory function of Ena/VASP on lamellipodial filaments was consistent with their clear relevance in the movement through the host cell cytosol of Listeria harboring the Ena/VASP ligand ActA (Geese et al., 2002; Loisel et al., 1999; Skoble et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both inhibitory and stimulatory roles of Ena/VASP on adhesion were reported.
source: Both inhibitory (Galler et al., 2006) and stimulatory roles (Gupton et al., 2012; Kang et al., 2010; Puleo et al., 2019; Young and Higgs, 2018) on adhesion were reported, whereas one study did not detect any effect in fibroblasts lacking Mena and VASP (Bear et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature showing conflicting results.

claim: One study did not detect any effect of Ena/VASP on adhesion in fibroblasts lacking Mena and VASP.
source: Both inhibitory (Galler et al., 2006) and stimulatory roles (Gupton et al., 2012; Kang et al., 2010; Puleo et al., 2019; Young and Higgs, 2018) on adhesion were reported, whereas one study did not detect any effect in fibroblasts lacking Mena and VASP (Bear et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Consecutive Ena/VASP member removal caused an increasing phenotype in 2D migration rate in B16-F1 cells.
source: Interestingly, consecutive Ena/VASP member removal caused an increasing phenotype in 2D migration rate, ranging from a modest reduction of 1.25 ± 0.37 µm/min and 1.19 ± 0.47 µm/min for single Evl KO mutants (E-KO) as compared to control (1.44 ± 0.4 µm/min), to 0.62 ± 0.25 µm/min and 0.57 ± 0.27 µm/min in Evl and VASP double-KOs (EV-KO), and 0.47 ± 0.19 µm/min and 0.43 ± 0.22 µm/min in triple-KOs (EVM-KO) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Single Evl KO mutants showed migration rates of 1.25 ± 0.37 µm/min and 1.19 ± 0.47 µm/min compared to control at 1.44 ± 0.4 µm/min.
source: Interestingly, consecutive Ena/VASP member removal caused an increasing phenotype in 2D migration rate, ranging from a modest reduction of 1.25 ± 0.37 µm/min and 1.19 ± 0.47 µm/min for single Evl KO mutants (E-KO) as compared to control (1.44 ± 0.4 µm/min), to 0.62 ± 0.25 µm/min and 0.57 ± 0.27 µm/min in Evl and VASP double-KOs (EV-KO), and 0.47 ± 0.19 µm/min and 0.43 ± 0.22 µm/min in triple-KOs (EVM-KO) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Evl and VASP double-KO mutants showed migration rates of 0.62 ± 0.25 µm/min and 0.57 ± 0.27 µm/min.
source: Interestingly, consecutive Ena/VASP member removal caused an increasing phenotype in 2D migration rate, ranging from a modest reduction of 1.25 ± 0.37 µm/min and 1.19 ± 0.47 µm/min for single Evl KO mutants (E-KO) as compared to control (1.44 ± 0.4 µm/min), to 0.62 ± 0.25 µm/min and 0.57 ± 0.27 µm/min in Evl and VASP double-KOs (EV-KO), and 0.47 ± 0.19 µm/min and 0.43 ± 0.22 µm/min in triple-KOs (EVM-KO) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Triple-KO mutants showed migration rates of 0.47 ± 0.19 µm/min and 0.43 ± 0.22 µm/min.
source: Interestingly, consecutive Ena/VASP member removal caused an increasing phenotype in 2D migration rate, ranging from a modest reduction of 1.25 ± 0.37 µm/min and 1.19 ± 0.47 µm/min for single Evl KO mutants (E-KO) as compared to control (1.44 ± 0.4 µm/min), to 0.62 ± 0.25 µm/min and 0.57 ± 0.27 µm/min in Evl and VASP double-KOs (EV-KO), and 0.47 ± 0.19 µm/min and 0.43 ± 0.22 µm/min in triple-KOs (EVM-KO) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from time-lapse microscopy shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Consecutive Ena/VASP removal was accompanied by a gradual increase in directionality culminating in EVM-KO cells that were 46% more directional than wild-type B16-F1.
source: This was accompanied by a gradual increase in directionality culminating in EVM-KO cells that were 46% more directional as compared to wild-type B16-F1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The frequency of turning angles at 0° increased from 10.2% in wild-type to 12.3% in single KO, 16.1% in double KO and 16.9% in triple KO cells.
source: Quantitative analyses of the turning angles revealed an incrementally increased frequency at 0° from 10.2% in wild-type to 12.3% in single KO, 16.1% in double KO and 16.9% in triple KO cells, in support of the higher directionality in mutant cells that coincided with their reduced motility (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Re-expression of VASP largely rescued cell speed, directionality and frequency of turning angles in EVM-KO cells.
source: Re-expression of VASP, which was found to contribute most efficiently to motility, largely rescued cell speed, directionality and frequency of turning angles (Figure 1E–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Rescue experiments with EGFP-tagged Evl or Mena yielded similar results to VASP, but these proteins were slightly less effective in restoring cell speed.
source: The rescue experiments with EGFP-tagged Evl or Mena yielded similar results, but these proteins were slightly less effective in restoring cell speed (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: All Ena/VASP mutant cells displayed incrementally decreasing and lower MSD values as compared to control.
source: Despite their higher directionality, presumably owing to their considerably slower motility, all Ena/VASP mutant cells displayed incrementally decreasing and lower MSD values as compared to control (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: In EVM-KO cells rescued with EGFP-tagged VASP, Evl or Mena, the MSD values were markedly increased.
source: Notably, in EVM-KO cells rescued with EGFP-tagged VASP, Evl or Mena, the MSD values were again markedly increased (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: No significant differences in invasion rates were found between EVM-KO and B16-F1 control cells in 3D Matrigel invasion assays.
source: Surprisingly, however, at least with the assay conditions employed, we did not find any significant differences in invasion rates between these cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The robust, Ena/VASP-driven promotion of actin-based protrusion is less important for migration in confinement.
source: However, although the mechanistic details of this result remain to be established, it suggests, at least, that the robust, Ena/VASP-driven promotion of actin-based protrusion is less important for migration in confinement, which particularly relies on actomyosin contractility, as previously reported for other cell types (Poincloux et al., 2011; Ramalingam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 3D invasion data, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: F-actin content in lamellipodia was reduced by about 45% in EVM-KO cells.
source: Quantification of F-actin contents in lamellipodia revealed about 45% reduction in the triple mutant, and the average width of lamellipodia was diminished by about 65% to 0.8 ± 0.2 µm when compared to wild-type with 2.3 ± 0.7 µm.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of phalloidin staining data.

claim: The average width of lamellipodia was diminished by about 65% to 0.8 ± 0.2 µm in EVM-KO cells compared to wild-type with 2.3 ± 0.7 µm.
source: Quantification of F-actin contents in lamellipodia revealed about 45% reduction in the triple mutant, and the average width of lamellipodia was diminished by about 65% to 0.8 ± 0.2 µm when compared to wild-type with 2.3 ± 0.7 µm.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of phalloidin staining data.

claim: In mutant cells reconstituted with EGFP-VASP, F-actin intensity increased 40% above wild-type levels.
source: In mutant cells reconstituted with EGFP-VASP, F-actin intensity increased even 40% above wild-type levels, and lamellipodium width was readily restored to 2.7 ± 0.8 µm (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: Lamellipodium width was readily restored to 2.7 ± 0.8 µm in mutant cells reconstituted with EGFP-VASP.
source: In mutant cells reconstituted with EGFP-VASP, F-actin intensity increased even 40% above wild-type levels, and lamellipodium width was readily restored to 2.7 ± 0.8 µm (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: The EVM-KO triple mutant virtually lacked fascin-containing bundles.
source: Again, the triple mutant virtually lacked fascin-containing bundles, as opposed to wild-type and reconstituted mutants expressing VASP, despite unchanged global expression of fascin in the mutant (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D-G.

claim: Global expression of fascin was unchanged in the EVM-KO mutant.
source: Again, the triple mutant virtually lacked fascin-containing bundles, as opposed to wild-type and reconstituted mutants expressing VASP, despite unchanged global expression of fascin in the mutant (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Virtually complete loss of microspikes was observed only upon disruption of all three Ena/VASP family members.
source: Finally, we examined the gene dose-dependent requirement for Ena/VASP family members in microspike formation and found that virtually complete loss of microspikes was observed only upon disruption of all three family members (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: None of the potent filopodia inducers (Rif L77, mDia2ΔDAD, FMNL3 E275, FMNL2 E272, or myosin X) were able to restore microspike-containing lamellipodia in EVM-KO cells.
source: Strikingly, none of the agents established previously to be capable of inducing filopodia formation, that is constitutively active variants of the small Rho GTPase Rif (L77), the formins mDia2 (mDia2ΔDAD), FMNL3 (E275) and to lesser extent FMNL2 (E272), or unconventional myosin X were able to restore microspike-containing lamellipodia, indicating that microspike formation requires more specific activities that are critically dependent on Ena/VASP function (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Microspike formation requires more specific activities that are critically dependent on Ena/VASP function.
source: Strikingly, none of the agents established previously to be capable of inducing filopodia formation, that is constitutively active variants of the small Rho GTPase Rif (L77), the formins mDia2 (mDia2ΔDAD), FMNL3 (E275) and to lesser extent FMNL2 (E272), or unconventional myosin X were able to restore microspike-containing lamellipodia, indicating that microspike formation requires more specific activities that are critically dependent on Ena/VASP function (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the inability of various filopodia inducers to rescue microspikes in EVM-KO cells.

claim: Filopodia formation frequency per cell was reduced by 66% in EVM-KO cells compared to B16-F1 control on low laminin after CK666 treatment.
source: Analyses of phalloidin-stained cells revealed that albeit reduced in formation frequency per cell, filopodia formation was still possible in EVM-KO cells (66% compared to B16-F1 control on low laminin).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of filopodia in CK666-treated cells.

claim: Filopodia can form to significant extent without lamellipodia upon inhibition of Arp2/3 complex.
source: At the same time, these data also illustrated that filopodia can indeed form to significant extent without lamellipodia, for example upon inhibition of Arp2/3 complex and thus in the absence of microspikes (Figure 4B–C, Figure 4—source data 1), in spite of the reduced frequencies of filopodia formation observed here.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Induction of filopodia formation by expression of constitutively active mDia2 was virtually identical in the EVM-KO mutant as compared to B16-F1 cells.
source: Conversely, however, induction of filopodia formation by expression of constitutively active mDia2 (Block et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2007) was virtually identical in the EVM-KO mutant as compared to B16-F1 cells (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—source data 1), supporting the view of multiple pathways leading to filopodium formation (Young et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Arp2/3 complex accumulated in a peripheral band much narrower than commonly observed in wild-type lamellipodia (reduced by 64%) in EVM-KO cells.
source: To explore if or how loss of Ena/VASP function affected Arp2/3 complex accumulation, we immunolabeled the cells for the Arp2/3 complex and found that it accumulated in a peripheral band much narrower than commonly observed in wild-type lamellipodia (reduced by 64%), but with roughly 75% higher intensity at the tips of mutant lamellipodia (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Arp2/3 complex intensity was roughly 75% higher at the tips of mutant lamellipodia in EVM-KO cells.
source: To explore if or how loss of Ena/VASP function affected Arp2/3 complex accumulation, we immunolabeled the cells for the Arp2/3 complex and found that it accumulated in a peripheral band much narrower than commonly observed in wild-type lamellipodia (reduced by 64%), but with roughly 75% higher intensity at the tips of mutant lamellipodia (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: CP and cortactin distributions were much narrower (reduced by 60% and 67%, respectively) in EVM-KO cells.
source: CP and cortactin distributions were highly reminiscent of changes in Arp2/3, again much narrower (reduced by 60% and 67%, respectively), and with approximately 75% and 60% increased intensities in EVM-KO as compared to controls (Figure 5D–F, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-I.

claim: CP and cortactin intensities were approximately 75% and 60% increased in EVM-KO as compared to controls.
source: CP and cortactin distributions were highly reminiscent of changes in Arp2/3, again much narrower (reduced by 60% and 67%, respectively), and with approximately 75% and 60% increased intensities in EVM-KO as compared to controls (Figure 5D–F, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–I).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D-F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-I.

claim: No noticeable difference in distribution and intensity of WAVE2 was found in wild-type versus EVM-KO cells.
source: Interestingly, we found no noticeable difference in distribution and intensity of WAVE2 in wild-type versus EVM-KO (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J–L).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J-L.

claim: Lamellipodia protrusion was reduced by 35% in EVM-KO cells as compared to control or EVM-KO rescued with EGFP-VASP.
source: Quantification revealed lamellipodia protrusion to be reduced by 35% in EVM-KO cells as compared to control or EVM-KO rescued with EGFP-VASP (Figure 5I, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by kymograph analysis data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Lamellipodia persistence was at best slightly reduced in EVM-KO cells, but not in a statistically significant fashion.
source: Notably, despite reduced protrusion, lamellipodia persistence was at best slightly reduced in EVM-KO cells, but not in a statistically significant fashion (Figure 5J), confirming that protrusion effectivity can be readily uncoupled from persistence (Block et al., 2012; Kage et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J and citations to prior literature.

claim: Lamellipodial actin network translocation was reduced by about 22% in EVM-KO as compared to B16-F1 controls.
source: Lamellipodial actin network translocation was also reduced by about 22% in EVM-KO as compared to B16-F1 controls, suggesting that the effects on protrusion described above can be explained, at least in part, by reduced actin network polymerization (Figure 5L, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: EVM-deficient lamellipodia contained much sparser and less organized filament networks compared to wild-type cells.
source: In contrast to lamellipodia of wild-type cells, EVM-deficient lamellipodia contained much sparser and less organized filament networks (Figure 6A, Figure 6—video 1), which is consistent with the F-actin stainings in Figure 3A–B.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Actin filaments in the front region of EVM-KO lamellipodia were considerably shorter than in wild-type.
source: Consistently, assessment of actin filaments in the front region (within a ~ 1 µm broad zone behind the edge) revealed considerably shorter filaments in the mutant (Figure 6B, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Toward the interior of the lamellipodium, filament density in the EVM-mutant decreased noticeably faster as compared to control.
source: Moreover, toward the interior of the lamellipodium, filament density in the EVM-mutant decreased noticeably faster as compared to control, while at the edge, barbed ends occurred in excess in the mutant (Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: At the edge, barbed ends occurred in excess in the EVM-mutant.
source: Moreover, toward the interior of the lamellipodium, filament density in the EVM-mutant decreased noticeably faster as compared to control, while at the edge, barbed ends occurred in excess in the mutant (Figure 6C, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Pointed end densities were significantly above control values in particular within the first half micron of the edge in EVM-KO cells.
source: Consistent with reduced filament lengths (Figure 6B) and increased Arp2/3 intensities at the edge of EVM-KO cells (Figure 5A–B), assessed pointed end densities were significantly above control values in particular within the first half micron of the edge (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The distribution of filament angles in EVM-deficient lamellipodia was distinct, with the 90° peak being 17% lower than in control.
source: Finally, although both control and mutant lamellipodia exhibited a wide array of filament angles abutting the protruding front, with a clear maximum around 90° relative to the edge (Figure 6D, Figure 6—source data 1), the distribution of filament angles in EVM-deficient lamellipodia was distinct, with the 90° peak being clearly less prominent (17% lower than in control).
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Filament fractions with diagonal angles were about doubled in EVM-deficient lamellipodia compared to controls.
source: Conversely, filament fractions with diagonal angles were about doubled compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by electron tomography data analyzing filament angles.

claim: Reduced filament mass and disordered filament network geometry in the EVM-mutant are causative for reduced protrusion and network assembly.
source: These data suggest that reduced filament mass and disordered filament network geometry in the mutant are causative for reduced protrusion and network assembly.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the electron tomography data.

claim: MVE-KO cells displayed a substantial spreading defect that was fully rescued by Evl re-expression.
source: Notably, MVE-KO cells displayed a substantial spreading defect that was fully rescued by Evl re-expression (Figure 7B–C, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Untransfected MVE-KO cells formed noticeably smaller FAs on average than the same cells expressing distinct Ena/VASP family members.
source: Untransfected MVE-KO cells formed noticeably smaller FAs on average than the same cells expressing distinct Ena/VASP family members, but the rescue with Evl appeared most effective (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Rescue with Evl appeared most effective for FA formation in MVE-KO cells.
source: Untransfected MVE-KO cells formed noticeably smaller FAs on average than the same cells expressing distinct Ena/VASP family members, but the rescue with Evl appeared most effective (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Vinculin intensity was reduced by almost 30% in MVE-KO cells as compared to the parental MVD7 cell line.
source: Notably however, vinculin intensity was clearly reduced in the triple mutant by almost 30% as compared to the parental MVD7 cell line, and again fully rescued by Evl expression, while rescue of MVE-KO cells with VASP or Mena was less effective (Figure 7F, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by focal adhesion analysis data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Vinculin intensity in MVE-KO cells was fully rescued by Evl expression.
source: Notably however, vinculin intensity was clearly reduced in the triple mutant by almost 30% as compared to the parental MVD7 cell line, and again fully rescued by Evl expression, while rescue of MVE-KO cells with VASP or Mena was less effective (Figure 7F, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by focal adhesion analysis data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Rescue of MVE-KO cells with VASP or Mena was less effective than Evl for vinculin intensity.
source: Notably however, vinculin intensity was clearly reduced in the triple mutant by almost 30% as compared to the parental MVD7 cell line, and again fully rescued by Evl expression, while rescue of MVE-KO cells with VASP or Mena was less effective (Figure 7F, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by focal adhesion analysis data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: FA size in MVE-KO cells was reduced by 18% as compared to MVD7 cells.
source: Consistently, FA size in MVE-KO cells was reduced by 18% as compared to MVD7 cells (Figure 7G, Figure 7—source data 1), despite the low abundance of Evl in this cell line (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by focal adhesion analysis data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Expression of VASP or Mena in MVE-KO cells increased FA size only by 11% or 16%, respectively.
source: Furthermore, expression of VASP or Mena in MVE-KO cells increased FA size only by 11% or 16%, respectively, while expression of Evl increased FA size by more than 24%.
evidence: This is supported by focal adhesion analysis data.

claim: Expression of Evl in MVE-KO cells increased FA size by more than 24%.
source: Furthermore, expression of VASP or Mena in MVE-KO cells increased FA size only by 11% or 16%, respectively, while expression of Evl increased FA size by more than 24%.
evidence: This is supported by focal adhesion analysis data.

claim: Evl expression was most efficient in rescuing the average number of FAs per cell compared to VASP and Mena.
source: Accordingly, Evl expression was most efficient in rescuing the average number of FAs per cell as compared to VASP and Mena (Figure 7H, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by focal adhesion analysis data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: B16-F1-derived EVM-KO cells spread considerably slower than wild-type or reconstituted mutant cells expressing either EGFP-tagged VASP or Evl.
source: Consistent with the removal of Evl in MVD7 fibroblasts, B16-F1-derived EVM-KO cells also spread considerably slower than wild-type or reconstituted mutant cells expressing either EGFP-tagged VASP or Evl (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by spreading assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Evl rescued spreading more effectively than VASP in B16-F1 EVM-KO cells.
source: In these experiments, once more, Evl rescued more effectively than VASP (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by spreading assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: EVM-KO cells showed diminished vinculin intensity in FAs as well as reduced FA size and length compared to B16-F1 control cells.
source: Additionally, we also compared various adhesion parameters in EVM-KO and B16-F1 control cells and observed diminished vinculin intensity in FAs as well as reduced FA size and length (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: This is supported by focal adhesion analysis data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-H.

claim: Evl showed a moderate, but statistically significant increase in the amount of immobile fraction in focal adhesions as compared to VASP.
source: Notably, Evl showed a moderate, but statistically significant increase in the amount of immobile fraction in focal adhesions as compared to VASP, potentially explaining its more robust accumulation in these structures as compared to EGFP-tagged VASP (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B, Figure 7—video 2).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: No differences between Evl and VASP were observed for their turnover rates in focal adhesions or lamellipodia.
source: No differences, however, between these proteins were observed for their turnover rates, neither in focal adhesions nor lamellipodia (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C–D, Figure 7—video 3), suggesting that the observed, functional relevance of Evl in focal adhesions may indeed derive from its more stable association with specific focal adhesion components.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C-D.

claim: Evl appeared more critical in the regulation of cell-substrate adhesions despite clearly overlapping functions of Ena/VASP proteins.
source: Together, despite clearly overlapping functions of Ena/VASP proteins in various actin-dependent processes, Evl appeared more critical in the regulation of cell-substrate adhesions.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on multiple adhesion-related experiments.

claim: The contractile energy was significantly reduced in MVE-KO cells as compared to MVD7.
source: Interestingly, the contractile energy was significantly reduced in MVE-KO cells as compared to MVD7 (Figure 8B–C, Figure 8—source data 1), and rescued upon stable expression of EGFP-tagged Evl (Figure 8D–E, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by traction force microscopy data shown in Figure 8B-C.

claim: Contractile energy was rescued in MVE-KO cells upon stable expression of EGFP-tagged Evl.
source: Interestingly, the contractile energy was significantly reduced in MVE-KO cells as compared to MVD7 (Figure 8B–C, Figure 8—source data 1), and rescued upon stable expression of EGFP-tagged Evl (Figure 8D–E, Figure 8—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by traction force microscopy data shown in Figure 8D-E.

claim: The contractile energies of Evl-rescued MVE-KO and parental MVD7 cells were highly similar to each other.
source: Moreover, the contractile energies of Evl-rescued MVE-KO and parental MVD7 cells were highly similar to each other.
evidence: This is supported by traction force microscopy data.

claim: Comparable results for contractile energy were obtained with unconfined cells on homogenous fibronectin coating.
source: Comparable results were obtained with unconfined cells, i.e. homogenous fibronectin coating on polyacrylamide substrata, and thus in the absence of size- and geometry-specific constraints (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by traction force microscopy data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Ena/VASP proteins positively regulate 2D cell migration of distinct mesenchymal cell types.
source: At variance to earlier studies (Bear et al., 2002; Bear et al., 2000; Loureiro et al., 2002), we show that Ena/VASP proteins positively regulate 2D cell migration of distinct mesenchymal cell types, since their consecutive loss in B16-F1 cells results in cumulative, reconstitutable motility phenotypes.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript and contrasts with prior literature.

claim: The reduced net cell translocation rates in EVM-KOs occur because of reduced lamellipodial actin assembly and protrusion rates.
source: Thus, despite increased directionality, the reduced net cell translocation rates observed in EVM-KOs as compared to wild-type occur because of reduced lamellipodial actin assembly and protrusion rates.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on multiple experimental observations including FRAP and protrusion rate measurements.

claim: Ena/VASP operate in a mechanistically conserved fashion at least in adhesive, 2D migration.
source: Diminished migration was also observed in MVD7 fibroblasts after genetic removal of Evl as well as in NIH 3T3 fibroblast after consecutive disruption of Mena and VASP, supporting the view that Ena/VASP operate in a mechanistically conserved fashion at least in adhesive, 2D migration, reconciling previous controversies (Auerbuch et al., 2003; Geese et al., 2002; Lacayo et al., 2007; Loisel et al., 1999; Rottner et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on consistent findings across multiple cell types and reconciles prior conflicting literature.

claim: The absence of Ena/VASP may allow for an increased fraction of CP localizing to filament barbed ends in the lamellipodium tip.
source: During filament elongation, Ena/VASP proteins are thought to compete with CP for growing filament barbed ends (Bear et al., 2002; Breitsprecher et al., 2011a; Breitsprecher et al., 2008; Hansen and Mullins, 2010). One possibility therefore is that the absence of Ena/VASP may allow for an increased fraction of CP localizing to filament barbed ends in the lamellipodium tip.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known competition between Ena/VASP and CP.

claim: An increased amount of CP might increase the activity of Arp2/3 complex, as CP has been reported to operate as co-factor of Arp2/3-dependent actin assembly.
source: This effect might even be enhanced by the increase of barbed ends deduced from electron tomography data. An increased amount of CP might then be sufficient to increase the activity of Arp2/3 complex, as CP has also been reported to operate as co-factor of Arp2/3-dependent actin assembly (Akin and Mullins, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Overexpression of VASP in B16-F1 cells was previously found to increase F-actin, but decrease Arp2/3 complex intensities in lamellipodia.
source: In line with this view, overexpression of VASP in B16-F1 cells was previously found to increase F-actin, but decrease Arp2/3 complex intensities in lamellipodia (Dimchev et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Upon loss of Ena/VASP, filaments may become shorter and Arp2/3 complex intensities may increase due to enhanced branching activity.
source: Thus, upon loss of Ena/VASP, filaments may not only become shorter, but Arp2/3 complex intensities simply increase due to enhanced branching activity relative to growing actin networks, which would also be consistent with the shorter and more highly branched filaments previously observed by platinum replica EM upon mitochondrial Ena/VASP sequestration (Bear et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Increased Arp2/3 densities might indirectly contribute to the increase of its co-regulator CP.
source: In this alternative possibility, increased Arp2/3 densities might in turn indirectly contribute to the increase of its co-regulator CP (Akin and Mullins, 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Acute sequestration of Arp2/3 complex coincides with removal of both Arp2/3 complex and CP from lamellipodia.
source: The latter view is supported by the observation that acute, experimental sequestration of Arp2/3 complex, achieved by microinjection of recombinant WCA, coincides with removal of both Arp2/3 complex and CP from lamellipodia, suggesting that capping protein accumulation in the lamellipodium does indeed depend on the presence of Arp2/3 complex (Koestler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The increased accumulation of cortactin in mutant lamellipodia is consistent with the general coincidence of its subcellular positioning with Arp2/3 complex.
source: The increased accumulation of cortactin in mutant lamellipodia is consistent with the general coincidence of its subcellular positioning with Arp2/3 complex (Schnoor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: FMNL2/3 removal caused defects partly reminiscent of Ena/VASP deficiency, although phenotypes seen upon Ena/VASP deficiency were more severe.
source: Indeed, FMNL2/3 removal caused defects partly reminiscent of what's seen here, at least concerning impact on lamellipodial protrusion, actin filament densities or microspike formation (see below), although phenotypes seen upon Ena/VASP deficiency were more severe.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work suggesting partial functional overlap.

claim: The virtual absence of microspikes, but not of filopodia, in EVM-KO cells establishes fundamental differences between these molecular entities.
source: As yet, authors of even highly relevant literature have decided not to clearly distinguish between filopodia and microspikes to facilitate analyses of finger-like protrusions (Svitkina et al., 2003; Vignjevic et al., 2006). However, the virtual absence of microspikes, but not of filopodia, in EVM-KO cells combined with the inability of established filopodia inducers such as mDia2, FMNL3, myosin X and Rif to rescue microspikes clearly establishes, perhaps for the first time, fundamental differences between these molecular entities.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on experimental data distinguishing microspikes from filopodia.

claim: In contrast to filopodia, microspikes form exclusively by convergent elongation.
source: The findings provided here strongly suggest that in contrast to filopodia, microspikes form exclusively by convergent elongation, as previously suggested (Svitkina et al., 2003), whereas filopodia may emerge by multiple, distinct mechanisms (Young et al., 2015), opening a door for resolving a long-standing controversy in the field.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on experimental data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Filopodia may emerge by multiple, distinct mechanisms.
source: The findings provided here strongly suggest that in contrast to filopodia, microspikes form exclusively by convergent elongation, as previously suggested (Svitkina et al., 2003), whereas filopodia may emerge by multiple, distinct mechanisms (Young et al., 2015), opening a door for resolving a long-standing controversy in the field.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to prior literature.

claim: Ena/VASP proteins reside together with vinculin in the force-transduction layer in-between talin and ends of stress fiber filaments.
source: Ena/VASP proteins are well established to accumulate in FAs of adherent cells, and known to reside together with vinculin in the force-transduction layer in-between talin and ends of stress fiber filaments (Kanchanawong et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The binding of vinculin to F-actin is critical to its role in cell-matrix adhesion.
source: The binding of vinculin to F-actin is critical to its role in cell-matrix adhesion since disruptions of the vinculin-F-actin interaction affect cell morphology, cell motility and adhesion (Ezzell et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The underlying cause of defects from disrupting vinculin-F-actin interaction is the impaired ability to generate and transduce forces.
source: The underlying cause of these defects is apparently the impaired ability to generate and transduce forces (Mierke et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Vinculin-Ena/VASP complexes might synergize in the capture of filament barbed ends, to regulate force generation and transduction in FAs.
source: Moreover, since vinculin and VASP interact with each other (Brindle et al., 1996), vinculin-Ena/VASP complexes might synergize in the capture of filament barbed ends, to regulate force generation and transduction in FAs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on known interactions and supported by citation.

claim: Lack of Ena/VASP proteins consistently impairs integrin-dependent spreading and changes in FA patterns.
source: Here, we show that lack of Ena/VASP proteins consistently impairs integrin-dependent spreading and changes in FA patterns, and that from the three Ena/VASP family members, the rescue with Evl is most effective concerning relevant adhesion parameters.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on experimental data from spreading and FA analysis.

claim: From the three Ena/VASP family members, the rescue with Evl is most effective concerning relevant adhesion parameters.
source: Here, we show that lack of Ena/VASP proteins consistently impairs integrin-dependent spreading and changes in FA patterns, and that from the three Ena/VASP family members, the rescue with Evl is most effective concerning relevant adhesion parameters.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on experimental data from spreading and FA analysis.

claim: The particularly important role of Evl in adhesion is strengthened by diminished traction forces upon its disruption.
source: The particularly important role of Evl in adhesion is strengthened by diminished traction forces upon its disruption, and further supported by our FRAP data, implying that Evl is more stably associated with other focal adhesion components as compared to VASP.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on traction force microscopy and FRAP data.

claim: FRAP data imply that Evl is more stably associated with other focal adhesion components as compared to VASP.
source: The particularly important role of Evl in adhesion is strengthened by diminished traction forces upon its disruption, and further supported by our FRAP data, implying that Evl is more stably associated with other focal adhesion components as compared to VASP.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on FRAP data showing increased immobile fraction for Evl.

claim: The specialized role of Evl in integrin-dependent adhesion is consistent with very recent work showing its specific requirement for FA maturation, cell-matrix adhesion and mechanosensing.
source: The specialized role of Evl in integrin-dependent adhesion is consistent with very recent work showing its specific requirement for FA maturation, cell-matrix adhesion and mechanosensing (Puleo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent literature.

claim: Mena is by far the most abundant Ena/VASP protein present in both melanoma and fibroblast cell lines.
source: First, Mena is by far the most abundant protein present in both melanoma and fibroblast cell lines, but in particular considering this fact, phenotypes generated by its elimination are comparably modest.
evidence: This is based on quantification of cellular Ena/VASP protein concentrations.

claim: Phenotypes generated by Mena elimination are comparably modest despite its high abundance.
source: First, Mena is by far the most abundant protein present in both melanoma and fibroblast cell lines, but in particular considering this fact, phenotypes generated by its elimination are comparably modest.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison of expression levels and phenotypic effects.

claim: Mena might not sufficiently find its relevant, specific interactors that might promote its impact in structures like cell-cell contacts or tissues like the nervous system.
source: In spite of its abundance, we are tempted to speculate therefore that it simply does not sufficiently find its relevant, specific interactors that might promote its impact in other structures such as cell-cell contacts (Scott et al., 2006) or tissues like the nervous system (Kwiatkowski et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VASP is expressed at much higher levels compared to Evl, which by itself could explain its more prominent role in cell migration.
source: Notwithstanding this, VASP is still expressed at much higher levels compared to Evl, which by itself could explain its more prominent role in cell migration.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on quantification of cellular protein concentrations.
